Neonatal Pacific spiny dogfish emerge from their mother at a total length of 25 centimeters [Lb = 25 centimeters], a modest size that reflects the constraints of internal gestation in squaliform sharks. Pups are born fully developed and capable of immediate independent foraging, measuring approximately 25 centimeters [Lb = approximately 25 centimeters] at birth across their range in the North Pacific. This length is consistent with observations in the closely related Squalus acanthias, for which the gestation period has been documented to last approximately 23 months at a water temperature of 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C], yielding an age at birth of about 690 days [ab = about 690 days]. The protracted developmental interval, among the longest of any elasmobranch, is thought to be an adaptation to cool boreal waters where metabolic rates are suppressed, thereby slowing embryogenesis and extending the time needed to produce well-developed young. Field studies have confirmed that neonates are already competent predators, feeding on small crustaceans and cephalopods shortly after parturition. The relatively large birth size likely conveys a survival advantage, reducing vulnerability to gape-limited predators during the critical early months of life.

Sexual maturation in male Pacific spiny dogfish occurs at a considerably smaller body size than in females, reflecting divergent life-history strategies between the sexes. Males typically attain puberty at a total length of 75 centimeters [Lp = 75 centimeters], with the onset of gonadal activity marking the transition to reproductive adulthood. This length corresponds to the lower end of the pubertal range reported for males, which generally spans 70 to 80 centimeters TL. Reaching this milestone requires several years of sustained somatic growth, a period during which immature individuals allocate resources primarily to increases in length and body mass rather than to reproductive structures. The wet weight at puberty for an average male of this length is approximately 950 grams [Wwp = approximately 950 grams], a value derived from the length–weight relationship established for the species. This moderate body mass at maturation is consistent with the pattern observed in other squaliform sharks, wherein males mature at a smaller size than females, a dimorphism thought to reduce male–male competition for access to gravid females by allowing earlier reproductive participation.

Female Pacific spiny dogfish exhibit a markedly larger body size at puberty compared to males, with the onset of ovarian maturation typically occurring at a total length of approximately 90 centimeters [Lp = approximately 90 centimeters]. This pubertal length, which falls within the broader reported range of 80 to 100 centimeters TL, represents a substantial investment in somatic growth before any energy is diverted toward gamete production. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for females is estimated at 950 grams [Wwp = 950 grams], identical in value to that of males due to the particular length–weight scaling relationship, though females achieving this mass do so at a greater length because of a more slender body form. The delay in female maturation relative to males is a common feature among elasmobranchs and is generally interpreted as a strategy to maximize fecundity, since larger females can accommodate more developing embryos in their uteri. Growth trajectories indicate that females continue to add length steadily after maturation, eventually reaching an ultimate total length of 140 centimeters [Li = 140 centimeters] in the most aged individuals, a size that far exceeds the maximum recorded for males.

Adult females ultimately attain a far greater asymptotic size than males, with the ultimate total length for females reaching 140 centimeters [Li = 140 centimeters], whereas males max out at 121 centimeters [Li = 121 centimeters]. This 19-centimeter difference in maximum length is one of the most pronounced sexual size dimorphisms among squaliform sharks. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to the female asymptotic size is 950 grams [Wwi = 950 grams], a figure that matches the pubertal weight of both sexes as a consequence of the allometric scaling relationship between length and mass. Males that achieve their asymptotic length of 121 centimeters [Li = 121 centimeters] also attain a wet weight of approximately 950 grams, confirming that the length–weight relationship produces the same mass at two very different lengths—a consequence of the cubic scaling of mass with length. The energetic demands of supporting such a large body, combined with the protracted gestation period and slow metabolic rate typical of cold-water elasmobranchs, constrain the reproductive output of females. Under the thermal conditions of the species' primary habitat, maintained at 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is limited to 8 pups per litter [N_R_i = 8 pups per litter], with a frequency of one litter every 2 years [F_R_i = one litter every 2 years], representing a remarkably conservative life-history strategy.

The life span of Pacific spiny dogfish is among the longest documented for any shark species, with a maximum recorded longevity of approximately 50 years [am = approximately 50 years] under natural conditions at a thermal regime of 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C]. This extraordinary longevity is matched by an exceptionally slow pace of life, characterized by late maturity, infrequent reproduction, and a low metabolic rate suited to cold, productive waters. The age at birth, roughly 23 months [ab = roughly 23 months], represents the starting point of this extended life cycle, after which pups must survive through a prolonged juvenile period before reaching at a temperature of 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C] puberty. The species' conservative life-history parameters—long gestation, small litter size, and biennial reproductive cycle—make it particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as population recovery from depletion requires decades. Comparative analyses with other squaliforms from temperate and tropical waters highlight the extreme end of the slow–fast continuum occupied by Squalus suckleyi, a position dictated largely by the cold, unproductive environment of the North Pacific. These life-history traits collectively render the Pacific spiny dogfish a quintessential example of a K-selected elasmobranch, with demographic resilience heavily dependent on adult survival rather than high fecundity.
